The app itself

Loading Splitzy…

How it works

Three steps, one honest number

Splitzy does one job: keep a running ledger of a shared group and say, at any moment, exactly who owes whom how much to make it even. It walks in three moves.

  1. Add the people

    Name everyone in the group — roommates, trip mates, whoever was at the table. Remove someone later and Splitzy cleans up their rows so the maths never lies.

  2. Log who paid what

    One expense at a time: who fronted the money, the amount, and who shares it. Amounts are unit-free on purpose — rupees, dollars or shells, the split is the same.

  3. Read the settle-up list

    Balances appear live, and the settle-up panel proposes a short list of payments — “Chen pays Ana 9.83” — that squares everyone with as little moving money as the method can manage.

The maths behind it

Two pass-offs over an even split

Step one: a net balance per person

For every expense, Splitzy divides the amount equally among the people you ticked, then walks the whole list and keeps one number per person: everything they paid, minus everything they owe. Positive means the group owes them; negative means they owe the group. By construction these balances sum to zero — every rupee paid is a rupee someone owes. In code this is computeBalances() in js/app.jsx, re-derived from scratch on every change and memoized with useMemo, so there is no stale total to drift.

Step two: a greedy settle-up suggestion

The settle list is the classic greedy pairing: sort the people who are owed from highest down, the people who owe from highest down, and let the biggest debtor pay the biggest creditor as much as they can. Each payment zeroes out at least one person, so the list never needs more transfers than there are people with an open balance minus one. That is computeTransfers().

An honest caveat. “The fewest possible payments” is a harder problem than it looks, and greedy pairing is a heuristic, not a proof: it gives a short list, not always the provably shortest one, and a minimum-transfer set isn’t unique anyway — different orderings can settle the same group in the same number of payments. Splitzy’s job is to suggest a small, obvious list to act on — not to claim it is the only correct answer. Half-cent noise is handled with an epsilon (0.005), and displayed figures are rounded to two decimals, so a settled group may show a cent of rounding dust.

Why React, and what it cost

A demo’s trade-offs, written down

I reached for React on Splitzy because the app is almost entirely derived state: two lists in, balances and a settle plan out. Hooks, context and useMemo are exactly the tools for that shape — no prop-drilling through the panels, no hand-written re-render logic, and the money maths stays in plain, testable functions outside the component tree. The app demonstrates all of it deliberately.

What it costs, stated honestly: this page loads React 18 from a CDN and compiles js/app.jsx in the browser with Babel standalone. That means no build step, no bundler, no minification and no code splitting — a few hundred extra KB of tooling on every visit and JSX compiled at runtime. Fine for a demo you poke at for five minutes. Not what I’d ship to a client: there, the same code goes through Vite, gets pre-compiled, hashed and split like everyone expects.

The rest of the boundaries are equally deliberate:

  • No backend by design. Your group lives in localStorage in your own browser — nothing is uploaded, nothing syncs between devices, and clearing site data clears the ledger.
  • Currency amounts are unit-free numbers. No exchange rates, no symbol guessing: a demo of the maths, not of i18n.
  • Equal splits only. Percentage or share-weighted splitting is the obvious next feature; shipping without it is a scope choice, not an oversight.
